### Part A: Importing and Inspecting a CSV
```{r}
#A1 Import employees.csv into a data frame named emp_df using read.csv() with stringsAsFactors = FALSE.

emp_df<-read.csv("employees.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#A2 Display the structure, the first 5 rows, and summary of emp_df.
str(emp_df)
head(emp_df, 5)
summary(emp_df)
```

```{r}
#A3 Print the number of rows and the number of columns of emp_df, and the class of every column.
sapply(emp_df, class)
```
```{r}
#A4 Print the mean salary, the maximum age, and the number of employees in each department using table()
mean(emp_df$salary, na.rm = TRUE)
max(emp_df$age, na.rm = TRUE)
table(emp_df$department)
```
### Part B: Creating Data Frames
```{r}
#B1 Create a data frame new_hires with the same column names as emp_df and these three employees:
new_hires<-data.frame(
  emp_id = c(21, 22, 23),
  name = c("Uma", "Victor", "Wen"),
  department = c("HR", "IT", "Sales"),
  sex = c("F", "M", "F"),
  age = c(28, 37, 33),
  salary = c(45000, 83000, 60000),
  years_service = c(2, 9, 6),
  rating = c(3, 4, 5)
)
```

```{r}
#B2 Use rbind() to append new_hires to emp_df, saving the result as emp_all.
emp_all<-rbind(emp_df, new_hires)
dim(emp_all)
```

```{r}
#B3 Add a column bonus to emp_all equal to 5% of salary, rounded to the nearest whole number.
emp_all$bonus<-round(emp_all$salary*0.05)
```

### Part C: Subsetting
```{r}
#C1 Extract the first 5 rows and only the columns name and salary, using numeric or name indexing.
emp_all[1:5, c("name", "salary")]
```

```{r}
#C2 Using logical subsetting, select all employees with salary greater than 7000.
emp_all[emp_all$salary > 70000, ]
```

```{r}
#C3 Using subset function, select employees in the "IT" department with years_service of at least 5. Return only name, years_service and salary.
subset(emp_all, department == "IT" & years_service >= 5, select = c(name, years_service, salary))
```

```{r}
#C4 Use which() to print the row numbers of employees older than 50, then print their names.
older_idx <- which(emp_all$age > 50)
print(older_idx)
emp_all$name[older_idx]
```

```{r}
#C5 Remove the columns emp_id and bonus using negative indexing. Do not overwrite emp_all; print the first 3 rows of the result.
rem_df <- emp_all [, -c(1, 9)]
head(rem_df, 3)
```

```{r}
#C6 (2) Using logical indexing, print the salary of the employee whose name is "Mia".
emp_all$salary[emp_all$name == "Mia"]
```

### Part D: Factors
```{r}
#D1 Convert department and sex in emp_all to factors with factor(). Print levels() of each.
emp_all$department <- as.factor(emp_all$department)
emp_all$sex <- as.factor(emp_all$sex)
levels(emp_all$department)
levels(emp_all$sex)
```

```{r}
#D2 Use table() to count employees per department, and make a two-way table pf department by 'sex'.
table(emp_all$department)
table(emp_all$department, emp_all$sex)
```

```{r}
#D3 Create an ordered factor rating_level from rating using factor() with levels = 1:5 and labels = c("Poor", "Fair", "Good", "Very Good", "Excellent"). Add it to emp_all and print table(emp_all$rating_level)
emp_all$rating_level <- factor(emp_all$rating, levels = 1:5, 
                               labels = c("Poor", "Fair", "Good", "Very Good", "Excellent"), 
                               ordered = TRUE)
table(emp_all$rating_level)
```

```{r}
#D4 Using a for loop over levels(emp_all$department) and logical subsetting, print the mean salary of each department, rounded, to the nearest whole number.
for (dept in levels(emp_all$department)) {
  dept_salaries <- emp_all$salary[emp_all$department == dept]
  cat(dept, ":", round(mean(dept_salaries, na.rm = TRUE)), "\n")
}
```

### Part E: Conditional Statements
```{r}
#E1 Using nested ifelse(), add a column salary_band to emp_all: "High" if salary >= 70000, "Medium" if salary >= 50000 (and below 70000), otherwise "Low". Print table (eml_all$salary_band)
# E1: Using nested ifelse(), add salary_band to emp_all and print table
emp_all$salary_band <- ifelse(emp_all$salary >= 70000, "High",
                       ifelse(emp_all$salary >= 50000, "Medium", "Low"))
table(emp_all$salary_band)

```

```{r}
#E2 Using ifelse(), add a column level to emp_all: "Senior" if years_service is >= 8, otherwise "Junior". Print table(emp_all$level)
emp_all$level <- ifelse(emp_all$years_service >= 8, "Senior", "Junior")
table(emp_all$level)
```

```{r}
#E3 write a function raise_pct(rating) that uses an if/else if/else chain and returns 0.10 for a rating of 5, 0.07 for 4, 0.04 for 3, and 0 otherwise. Use sapply() to apply it to emp_all$rating, saving the result as a column raise. Then add a new_salary = round(salary*(1+raise)). Print the first 5 rows of name, rating, raise, new_salary.
raise_pct <- function(rating) {
  if (rating == 5) {
    return(0.10)
  } else if (rating == 4) {
    return(0.07)
  } else if (rating == 3) {
    return(0.04)
  } else {
    return(0)
  }
}
emp_all$raise <- sapply(emp_all$rating, raise_pct)
emp_all$new_salary <- round(emp_all$salary * (1 + emp_all$raise))
head(emp_all[, c("name", "rating", "raise", "new_salary")], 5)
```

```{r}
#E4 Using an if/else statement(not ifelse()), compute total <- sun(emp_all$new_salary) and print "Budget OK" if the total is below 1,600,000, otherwise print "Over budget". Also print the total.
total_new_sal <- sum(emp_all$new_salary)
if (total_new_sal < 1600000) {
  print("Budget OK")
} else {
  print("Over budget")
}
print(total_new_sal)
```

### Part F: Conditional Statements
```{r}
#F1 Uses sort() to print the 5 highest salary values in decreasing order, and the first 5 employe name values in alphabetical order.
head(sort(emp_all$salary, decreasing = TRUE), 5)
head(sort(emp_all$name), 5)
```

```{r}
#F2 Use order() to sort emp_all by salary in descending order and print the name, department and salary of the top 5. Save the sorted data frames as 'by_salary'.
# F2: Use order() to sort emp_all by salary in descending order and save top 5 to by_salary
by_salary <- emp_all[order(emp_all$salary, decreasing = TRUE), c("name", "department", "salary")][1:5, ]
print(by_salary)
```
